Neonatal Bactrian camels enter the world at a remarkably robust size, with newborns typically weighing around 34,000 grams [Wwb = around 34,000 grams]. This substantial birth mass, a common trait among large-bodied ungulates adapted to arid environments, provides the calf with essential energy reserves from the outset. The newborn, a precocial neonate, is soon standing and nursing, beginning a period of rapid growth fueled by the female's lipid-rich milk. Under the typical maternal body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], which supports optimal physiological function and milk synthesis, the calf remains in a state of complete nutritional dependence. This suckling stage concludes gradually, with the transition to a fully herbivorous diet and consequent nutritional independence occurring approximately 319 days after birth [tx = approximately 319 days after birth] at a temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This prolonged nursing period allows the calf to develop a robust rumen microbiome essential for digesting the tough, fibrous forage of its harsh habitat, a critical adaptation for survival in the steppes and deserts of Central Asia. Compared to other large-bodied ungulates such as the domestic cow (Bos taurus), in which weaning typically occurs at around 180 to 270 days, the extended suckling period of the Bactrian camel underscores the adaptive value of prolonged maternal investment in a resource-limited environment.

A female Bactrian camel reaches reproductive maturity after an extended period of somatic growth. Reported field studies indicate that the time from birth to the onset of puberty is approximately 1,278 days since birth [tp = approximately 1,278 days since birth], a duration that ensures the individual has attained sufficient body size and condition to support the energetic demands of gestation at a temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C] and lactation. This delayed maturation is characteristic of a slow life-history strategy, with females first conceiving around three and a half years of age. The gestation period itself is notably protracted; following a successful copulation, embryonic development proceeds over a period of 395 days [tg = 395 days] at a temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This lengthy gestation, measured under the stable core body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C] typical for the species, results in the birth of a single, highly developed calf. The considerable investment in each offspring reflects the challenges of rearing young in an environment where resources are unpredictable and often scarce, a pattern also observed in other large desert-adapted herbivores such as the Arabian oryx (Oryx leucoryx).

Adult body mass in the Bactrian camel exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males often being substantially larger than females. The ultimate wet weight for a typical adult female is frequently in the range of 350,000 grams [Wwi = 350,000 grams], a mass that facilitates efficient energy storage and thermoregulation in the extreme temperature fluctuations of Central Asian deserts. In contrast, a large dominant male can achieve an ultimate wet weight of 600,000 grams [Wwi = 600,000 grams], a size advantage that aids in intraspecific competition for access to breeding herds during the rut. This considerable difference in mass influences many aspects of their ecology, including daily food intake and territory defense. When considered against the neonatal mass, the overall growth trajectory from a 34-kilogram calf to a sexually mature adult represents a formidable energetic investment for both the individual and its mother, requiring multiple years of sustained foraging in often marginal pastures.

The reproductive output of the Bactrian camel is characterized by a low intrinsic rate, consistent with a long-lived species in a challenging environment. Females typically produce a single calf per reproductive event [N_R_i = single calf per reproductive event], and given the duration of gestation and a period of post-partum recovery, they generally achieve a maximum of one such event every two years [F_R_i = one such event every two years]. This low annual fecundity is linked to the considerable nutritional demands of lactation, which can delay the resumption of ovarian cycling. This conservative strategy prioritizes the survival of the individual calf and the condition of the mother, enhancing lifetime reproductive success over the species' extended lifespan. Compared to other camelids such as the dromedary (Camelus dromedarius), which may produce a calf every two years under optimal conditions, the reproductive schedule of the Bactrian camel is broadly similar, reflecting convergent adaptations to arid environments.

The Bactrian camel is a notably long-lived mammal, with a maximum lifespan in the wild and in captivity that reflects its slow life-history pace. Long-term datasets indicate that individuals can live for up to 12,921 days [am = up to 12,921 days], which is equivalent to approximately 35.4 years, when maintained under favorable conditions at a core body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This longevity, which is exceptional among large domestic ungulates, is supported by their robust physiology and ability to withstand extreme thermal and nutritional stress. However, typical lifespan estimates for free-ranging animals are more variable, with most individuals surviving between 15 and 25 years depending on predation pressure, drought severity, and disease prevalence. A characteristic sign of senescence in older animals includes progressive tooth wear, which eventually limits their ability to process coarse forage, leading to a slow decline in body condition and physiological deterioration that ultimately results in natural mortality.
